newsitem.title: USA: SBC asks US FCC to stay phone charge rules.
newsitem.headline: SBC asks US FCC to stay phone charge rules.

text.p: SBC Communications Inc said Wednesday it had asked the Federal Communications Commission to suspend its new rules overhauling the complex web of domestic phone charges.

The San Antonio, Texas-based Baby Bell also signaled it will go to court if the FCC -- as expected -- refuses to stay the rules, which cut the charges long-distance carriers pay to access the local phone network by $18.5 billion over five years.
"That would be the next step if we don't get any satisfaction from the FCC," an SBC spokesman said of the possible court action.
SBC would ask an appeals court to stay the rules while the court considers whether to overturn them. A legal challenge has been expected since the rules were approved last month.
SBC, the parent of Southwestern Bell Telephone Co, said the rules put the carrier at a competitive disadvantage and that some of its customers could face rate hikes as a result.
SBC has asked the FCC to make a decision on the carrier's request by June 11. An FCC spokeswoman said the agency had no comment.
Other Baby Bells -- including Ameritech Corp and BellSouth Corp -- said they are still reviewing the rules and have not decided whether to take legal action.
"We haven't decided what we're going to do," said Bob Bishop, a spokesman for GTE Corp. He said the carrier expects to support SBC's filing with the FCC.

GTE was among those that led the legal fight against the FCC's order last August opening the local phone market to competition. A U.S. appeals court in St. Louis is expected to rule soon on whether to overturn the "interconnection" rules.
A spokesman for No. 2 long-distance carrier MCI Communications Corp, meanwhile, criticized SBC's move.
"Southwestern Bell's request for the stay of the FCC's recent ... order demonstrates that once again the big Bell monopolies place monopoly profits ahead of consumer savings," said the spokesman.
"The stay request should be denied so consumers can more quickly gain the benefit of competition, lower prices, higher quality and greater choice."
